body.heading: An enzyme meets the air
paragraphs: Inside a whole apple, everything is separated and safe: the fruit's cells are intact, its chemicals are stored in compartments, and the skin keeps oxygen out. The chemistry of browning needs three things to meet — an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase, a family of colourless compounds called phenols, and oxygen — and a knife is what introduces them.

Cut or bruise the apple and the broken cells spill their contents together while air floods in. The enzyme immediately starts work, using the oxygen to convert the phenols through a series of steps into new compounds, which link up into large brown pigments called melanins — the same family of pigments that colours human skin and hair.

body.heading: Why the apple does it
paragraphs: Browning looks like decay, but it is probably a defence. The brown layer forms a seal over the wound, and the chemicals produced along the way taste bitter and discourage insects and microbes from moving in. A bruised apple is, in effect, bandaging itself.

The reaction needs all three ingredients, so removing any one of them slows it. It also explains the timing: browning races ahead in the first minutes after cutting, when oxygen and fresh-cut surfaces are plentiful, then settles into a slower creep.

body.heading: Stopping the brown
paragraphs: Kitchen wisdom maps neatly onto the chemistry. Lemon juice fights on two fronts — its vitamin C uses up oxygen before the enzyme can, and its acid makes the enzyme work sluggishly. Cling film and airtight boxes simply starve the reaction of oxygen, and a brief dip in water does the same.

Industry uses stronger versions of the same ideas, and breeders have gone further: 'Arctic' apples have been genetically engineered with the browning enzyme switched off, so a sliced apple stays pale for days. Whether or not you want your apples engineered, the brown blush on a cut apple is a small, visible chemical reaction you can watch — and stop — at home.

description: A sliced apple browns because cutting lets oxygen reach an enzyme that builds brown pigments — the fruit's own way of sealing a wound.
